newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST - Italy Sept PSBR seen at 21.0 trln lire.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Italy Sept PSBR seen at 21.0 trln lire.

text.p: Italy's September public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) is expected to be less than year ago levels, but the 1996 government target of 113 trillion lire still seems far off, a Reuter poll showed.
Analysts polled saw, on average, September PSBR at 21.0 trillion lire against 25.53 trillion lire in 1995.
Latest Bank of Italy data showed June PSBR at 24.72 trillion lire with the January-June cumulative PSBR at 52.19 trillion lire from 49.76 trillion lire in the same 1995 period.
August PSBR is forecast at some 8.5 trillion lire from 11.31 trillion lire in August 1995. July PSBR forecasts stand at 9.0 trillion lire against 5.9 trillion lire in 1995.

This would bring cumulative PSBR from January to September to some 91.0 trillion lire from 93.7 trillion lire in the same nine-month period of 1995. For 1996, analysts forecast a total borrowing requirement of 120 trillion lire.

One positive element seen for September's figure was lower debt financing costs. "The 1.0-1.5 trillion lire reduction in our PSBR forecast derives from lower debt financing costs," said Andrea Marchetti, analyst at Credito Italiano.
Also helping was the government's decision in June to cut funds to state railways and road maintainance company Anas.

Mario Noera of Deutsche Bank in Milan initially forecast PSBR at 23.6 trillion lire but said it "could fall to 21.0 trillion lire if the higher revenue that the 1996 mini-budget was supposed to bring in starts coming into effect."

Sonia Taraschi of Banca San Paolo di Torino said "September PSBR will be limited by the effects of the mini-budget which will allow the Treasury to save 2.0 trillion lire, and by the lower interest costs on Treasury paper."
Lower debt financing costs should also limit the overshoot of the government's 113.0 trillion lire target for 1996.
Credito Italiano's research office predicted debt servicing costs at 188.5 trillion lire from 195.3 trillion paid in 1995.
Deutsche Bank's research office saw these costs at 191.75 trillion lire.
"Debt servicing costs are falling less than forecast because BOTs (short term paper) and CCTs (floating rate certificates) feel the pinch of the tight monetary policy," Noera said.

Credito Italiano attributed the PSBR overshoot to lower-than-forecast revenues. "Of the 16.0 trillion lire of revenue that the mini-budget was supposed to create, only some 12.0-13.0 trillion lire will actually come in because some of the revenues were uncertain from the start," Marchetti said.
"It will be difficult for PSBR to drop under 120.0 trillion lire because of the lower-than-forecast gross domestic product growth," Chiara Fornasari of research body Prometeia said.

Italy's statistics body, Istat, said last Friday second-quarter GDP grew by 0.5 percent on a yearly basis from 1.5-percent growth in the previous quarter and shrank 0.5 percent on the quarter after rising 0.5 percent in the first three months.

"In the last part of the year, the benefits from lower interest rates and the effects of the mini-budget will be counterbalanced by the negative effects from a stagnating economy," Hugo Doyle of Banca Commerciale Italiana's (BCI) research office said.
Following are the analysts' forecasts (in trln lire)
SEPTEMBER 1996
Credito Italiano 23.0 118.0-119.0
Deutsche Bank Milan 21.0 115.0
Prometeia 21.0 120.0
Banca San Paolo di Torino 21.0 120.0
CONSENSUS 21.0 120.0
